title: Atlas API · release rollback
aliases: bad deployment failed deploy revert release rollback 503 after release
text:
# Release rollback — Atlas API 2.4

Scope: Atlas API version 2.4. Use this runbook when HTTP 503 responses increase immediately after a release. A time correlation is a hypothesis, not proof of the root cause.

First compare the release timestamp with the error-rate graph. Check readiness probes and the deployment event log. A failing readiness probe removes a replica from the serving pool.

If the new release is implicated and the database schema is backward compatible, the incident commander may approve reverting to the previous application revision. Check schema compatibility before rollback; a destructive migration makes an automatic rollback unsafe.

After an approved rollback, verify the HTTP 503 rate, healthy replica count, and request latency. Record the release revision and observed outcome in the incident timeline. This document does not authorize execution.

title: Atlas API · connection pool exhaustion
aliases: database db connections exhausted connection exhaustion pool saturated too many clients checkout timeout requests hanging
text:
# Database connection pool exhaustion — Atlas API 2.4

Symptoms include pool checkout timeouts and requests waiting for a database connection. Correlate active connections, pool wait time, and long-running transaction age before declaring connection pool exhaustion.

Inspect long-running transactions and connection leaks. Compare application concurrency with the database connection limit. Increasing the pool size without checking database capacity can worsen the incident.

Reduce incoming concurrency or shed nonessential work using the existing approved operational controls. Ask the database owner to review stale transactions before terminating any session.

Recovery checks: pool wait time returns to its normal range, request latency stabilizes, and database connections remain below the configured limit. Keep the incident open if the queue is still growing.

title: Atlas API · gateway timeout diagnosis
aliases: 504 gateway timeout slow upstream requests timing out
text:
# Gateway timeouts — Atlas API 2.4

A gateway HTTP 504 indicates that an upstream response exceeded the gateway timeout. Compare gateway duration with application request duration and dependency latency.

Use the request correlation identifier to follow a slow request through the application and its dependencies. Check database pool wait time separately from query execution time.

Do not increase the gateway timeout as the first fix. Establish which dependency is slow, check recent releases, and confirm whether a longer timeout would exhaust worker capacity.

title: Atlas API · credential rotation
aliases: 401 expired key rotate secret api token authentication unauthorized
text:
# Credential rotation — Atlas API 2.4

An HTTP 401 spike after credential rotation can indicate that some replicas still reference an old secret revision. Compare the deployed secret revision across replicas without printing secret values.

Confirm that the new credential is valid in the approved secret-management system. Follow the dual-credential rotation procedure where supported; revoke the old credential only after consumers have switched and the owner approves.

Never paste access tokens into incident chat, runbook uploads, model prompts, or diagnostic output. Record only the secret revision identifier and rotation timestamp.

title: Ledger worker · duplicate delivery
aliases: events arrive twice processed twice duplicate messages repeated event double delivery queue replay
text:
# Duplicate event delivery — Ledger worker 3.1

The queue provides at-least-once delivery, so the same event can be delivered more than once. A duplicate delivery does not by itself prove that two ledger writes occurred.

Inspect the event identifier and the idempotency record. The worker must write the idempotency record and ledger update in the same database transaction; acknowledge the message only after that transaction commits.

If the idempotency record is missing, pause a proposed replay and ask the ledger owner to investigate before reprocessing events. Never delete idempotency records to clear a backlog.

Validate the outcome by checking that one ledger mutation exists per event identifier. Queue depth alone is not a sufficient correctness check.

title: Ledger worker · poison messages
aliases: dead letter dlq poison message retry loop malformed payload backlog
text:
# Poison messages and the dead-letter queue — Ledger worker 3.1

A malformed payload can fail repeatedly and increase queue age. Compare the failing event identifiers, validation errors, retry count, and dead-letter queue depth.

Quarantine the failing event through the approved dead-letter path after the configured retry limit. Preserve the payload securely for investigation; redact personal data before sharing diagnostic examples.

Do not replay the entire dead-letter queue without determining the schema failure and reviewing idempotency behavior. Test a corrected payload in an isolated environment first.

aliases: bad deployment rollback revert failed deploy
text:
# Legacy rollback — Atlas API 1.8 ONLY

This procedure applies only to the retired version 1.8 deployment system. Its approval and migration assumptions differ from version 2.4.

For legacy rollback, the release owner must review the legacy migration journal and coordinate a maintenance window. Do not apply this procedure to Atlas API 2.4.
